name: Threat Modeling and Attack Surface
intent: Find what can go wrong before an attacker does: list what you protect, where input enters, where trust changes, then rank the threats and spend effort where it removes the most risk.
scenario: A small photo-sharing app has a web front end, an API, a database, a job queue with workers, an admin panel, a nightly backup and a build pipeline. The team has a few days to spend on security.
problem: Security work without a model is guesswork: teams fix what they already know how to fix, or what a scanner reports, and feel safe. Attackers use the parts nobody wrote down. Threat modeling is the habit of drawing the system, asking structured questions of every flow, and ranking the answers, so a limited budget goes to the threats that matter and the blind spots become visible.

howItWorks.title: List assets, entry points and trust boundaries
howItWorks.text: Assets are what an attacker wants: user photos, session tokens, the admin account, the database, the ability to run code on your servers. Entry points are every place data or commands come in: public endpoints, file uploads, a URL the server fetches, webhooks, queues, admin tools, the build pipeline. Trust boundaries are the lines where the level of trust changes, such as internet to API, API to database, or your code to a third-party library. A data-flow diagram with these three things marked is the whole model.

howItWorks.title: Ask STRIDE questions at each flow
howItWorks.text: STRIDE is six prompts: Spoofing (pretending to be someone), Tampering (changing data or code), Repudiation (denying an action with no proof either way), Information disclosure (seeing what you should not), Denial of service (making it unavailable) and Elevation of privilege (gaining rights you were not given). Use them as a checklist of questions for each flow that crosses a boundary, not as a form to fill in. Most flows have two or three real answers and several that do not apply, and that is fine.

howItWorks.title: Rank by likelihood and impact
howItWorks.text: Give each threat a rough likelihood and impact, such as 1 to 5 each, and multiply. The numbers are judgement calls and will be argued about; their job is to put threats in an order, not to measure anything. Likelihood depends on how easy the attack is and how many people can try it, impact on what the asset is worth and how far the damage spreads.

howItWorks.title: Choose fixes by risk removed per cost
howItWorks.text: List candidate mitigations and mark which threats each one removes. A single control often covers several threats, such as multi-factor authentication on both the login page and the admin panel, while another covers only one. Pick by the risk a fix removes per unit of effort, not by how easy or familiar it is. Then note what stays open and who accepts that on purpose.

howItWorks.title: Keep it small and repeat it
howItWorks.text: A model is a short document that changes with the system, not a one-off workshop. Revisit it when you add an entry point, a third party, a new data store or a new kind of user. Even a one-hour session around a whiteboard drawing, repeated at each significant design change, finds most of what a long formal exercise would.

pros: Puts effort where the risk is instead of where the tooling or habit points
Finds design flaws, such as a missing check between two services, that scanners and code review do not see
Cheap: a whiteboard, an hour and the people who built the system
Gives the team a shared, written reason for what was fixed and what was accepted
cons: Scores are opinions; two teams will rank the same threats differently
The model is only as good as the diagram, and a missing box is a missing threat
Goes stale when the system changes and nobody updates it
Can turn into a ritual that produces a long list nobody acts on
whenToUse: When designing a new feature that adds an entry point, a third-party integration or a new kind of data
Before a security budget is spent, so the money follows the risk
After an incident, to ask what else of the same shape exists in the system
whenNotToUse: As a substitute for fixing known, basic problems: patch, use parameterized queries and fix the obvious first
As a heavyweight gate for every small change, which teaches people to skip it
pitfalls: Modeling only what is easy to list: the public endpoints are on the OpenAPI file, but the admin panel, the build pipeline, the job queue, logs and backups are not, and they are where the damage often is
Treating STRIDE as a form to complete for every box rather than a set of prompts, so the output is long, shallow and unranked
Never ranking: twelve findings with no order get fixed in the order they were written down
Choosing fixes by ease, so the cheap ones are done first and the expensive, high-impact one is postponed forever
Counting a threat as handled because a control exists, without checking it covers every flow (login has rate limits but the admin login does not)
Drawing the model once and never again, so it describes last year's system
Forgetting the attacker already inside: a stolen employee laptop or a compromised dependency is a threat to model, not only strangers on the internet

roles.label: Team
roles.description: Draws the system and asks the questions.

roles.label: Data-flow model
roles.description: The written list of assets, entry points and boundaries.

roles.label: System
roles.description: What really runs, including the parts nobody drew.

roles.label: Attacker
roles.description: Uses whichever entry point is weakest.

quiz.question: A team lists every public API endpoint and fixes all the issues it finds there. A year later the breach comes through the admin panel, which was never on the list. What went wrong with the model?
options: It scored likelihood and impact on a 1 to 5 scale instead of using exact probabilities
It used STRIDE, which is too old to apply to modern systems
Its scope was what was easy to enumerate, so risk outside the drawn boundary was invisible
It listed too many endpoints, which buried the few important ones under noise
quiz.explanation: A model can only report on what was drawn. Easy-to-list things such as public endpoints get covered while admin tools, queues, build pipelines and backups are skipped. Rough scores are normal, and STRIDE is a prompt list, not something that expires.

quiz.question: Two fixes cost the same. One closes a threat scored 20 in a single flow. The other closes threats scored 12 and 10 in two flows. What is the sensible way to choose?
options: Take the one with the single highest score, because the worst single threat must always be closed first
Compare the total risk each removes for its cost, which favours the second, 22 against 20
Pick whichever the team knows how to implement fastest
Do neither until the scores are measured exactly
quiz.explanation: The goal is the most risk removed for the effort. A control that covers several flows can beat one that covers a single higher-scored flow. Scores are rough, but they are good enough to order decisions, so waiting for exact numbers only delays the fix.

quiz.question: A workshop walks through STRIDE for every box on the diagram and produces a 90-row spreadsheet. Six months later almost nothing has been changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: Nobody ranked the rows or tied them to fixes, so STRIDE was used as a form instead of a set of prompts
STRIDE finds too few threats per box to be worth the time of acting on any of them
The spreadsheet needed to be longer to cover every possible attack
Spoofing and tampering should have been left out of the model to keep it short
quiz.explanation: The value is in the order and the decisions that follow: which threats matter, which fix removes several, what is knowingly accepted. A long unranked list creates work without direction. More rows would not help.
